summary.text: Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) provides free energy to drive many processes in living cells, such as muscle contraction, nerve impulses and chemical synthesis.
Found in all known forms of life, it is often called the molecular unit of currency for energy transfer inside cells.
When used in a metabolic process ATP converts to ADP or AMP, and processes such as oxidative phosphorylation regenerate it.

facts.label: Daily turnover
facts.value: An adult recycles around 50 kilograms of ATP a day

facts.label: Three parts
facts.value: Adenine base, ribose sugar, and a triphosphate group

facts.label: Main eukaryote pathways
facts.value: Glycolysis, citric acid cycle with oxidative phosphorylation, beta-oxidation

facts.label: Yield per glucose
facts.value: Cellular respiration makes about 30 ATP from each glucose

facts.label: Stable pH range
facts.value: Stable in water between pH 6.8 and 7.4

items.prompt: A cell uses one molecule to power muscle contraction, nerve signals and building new compounds. Which role best fits that molecule?

options.label: A permanent building block of the cell's outer wall
A storage code recording the instructions for each task
A shared energy currency passed between many processes
A waste product that the cell clears after each task

items.explain: ATP drives many cell processes and is often called the molecular unit of currency for intracellular energy transfer.

items.prompt: A muscle cell spends ATP, which becomes ADP. What must happen for the cell to keep working?

options.label: The ADP is rebuilt into ATP, for example by oxidative phosphorylation
The ADP is excreted, and the cell takes up fresh ATP from food
The ADP is left alone, since it carries the same energy as ATP
The ADP is split into its sugar and base, which are then reused

items.explain: When ATP is consumed it converts to ADP or AMP, and processes such as oxidative phosphorylation or substrate-level phosphorylation regenerate it.

items.prompt: Glycolysis spends two ATP in its early steps and produces four ATP in its later steps. What is the net result?

options.label: A net loss of two ATP
A net gain of two ATP
No net change in ATP
A net gain of four ATP

items.explain: One ATP is invested in step 1 and another in step 3, then four are produced later, so a net of two ATPs is formed.

items.prompt: A non-photosynthetic aerobic eukaryote makes most of its ATP in one kind of structure. Which one?

options.label: The nucleus
The cell membrane
The ribosomes
The mitochondria

items.explain: ATP production by a non-photosynthetic aerobic eukaryote occurs mainly in the mitochondria.

items.prompt: ATP is stable in a near-neutral solution. What happens to it if the solution's pH becomes very extreme?

options.label: It becomes even more stable as the pH moves away
It converts into DNA and RNA building blocks
It rapidly hydrolyses to ADP and phosphate
It binds more metal ions and stays unchanged

items.explain: ATP is stable between pH 6.8 and 7.4, but at more extreme pH levels it rapidly hydrolyses to ADP and phosphate.

items.prompt: When a cell uses ATP in metabolism, which part of the molecule actually changes?

options.label: The triphosphate, which is trimmed to di- or monophosphate
The adenine, which is swapped for a different base
The ribose sugar, which is broken apart for fuel
All three parts, which are separated and rebuilt later

items.explain: In metabolic reactions the adenine and sugar stay unchanged while the triphosphate is converted to di- and monophosphate, giving ADP and AMP.

paragraphs.heading: The cell's energy coin
paragraphs.text: Adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, is a molecule that supplies the energy for many jobs in living cells, from contracting muscles and carrying nerve signals to building new chemicals. Every known form of life has it. Because cells use it to pass energy around inside themselves, it is often called the molecular unit of currency.

paragraphs.heading: Spending and recharging
paragraphs.text: When a cell uses ATP, its chain of three phosphates is cut down to two or one, turning it into adenosine diphosphate (ADP) or adenosine monophosphate (AMP). The adenine and the sugar stay the same throughout. Other processes, such as oxidative phosphorylation, then rebuild ATP. In aerobic metabolism this spending and rebuilding happens over and over again.

paragraphs.heading: A huge daily turnover
paragraphs.text: The amounts involved are large. An average adult makes and breaks down around 50 kilograms of ATP every day, which is about 100 moles. Living cells also hold the ratio of ATP to ADP ten orders of magnitude away from equilibrium. At the same time, they keep about five times as much ATP as ADP on hand.

paragraphs.heading: A magnesium partner
paragraphs.text: ATP carries several negative charges and grips metal ions tightly. Inside the cell it mostly exists bound to a magnesium ion, Mg²⁺, attached to oxygens on its phosphates. This magnesium strongly affects how ATP interacts with many proteins. ATP stays stable in water between pH 6.8 and 7.4, but at more extreme pH it quickly breaks down into ADP and phosphate.

paragraphs.heading: Where ATP comes from
paragraphs.text: In eukaryotes, ATP is made by three main pathways: glycolysis, the citric acid cycle together with oxidative phosphorylation, and beta-oxidation. The first two combined, which oxidize glucose all the way to carbon dioxide, are known as cellular respiration. They yield about 30 ATP from each glucose molecule. In eukaryotes that use oxygen and do not photosynthesize, most of this happens in the mitochondria, which fill nearly a quarter of a typical cell.

paragraphs.heading: Glycolysis step by step
paragraphs.text: Glycolysis breaks glucose and glycerol down into pyruvate, in two phases of five steps each. In the first, preparatory phase, the cell invests one ATP at step 1 and another at step 3, turning glucose into two molecules of a compound called g3p. In the second phase those two molecules become two pyruvates, and steps 7 and 10 each make two ATP from ADP. That leaves a net gain of two ATP. The pyruvate then feeds the citric acid cycle, which makes still more ATP.
